ety.text: From Middle English troute, troughte, trught, trouȝt, trouhte, partly from Old English truht (“trout”), and partly from Old French truite; both from Late Latin tructa, perhaps from Ancient Greek τρώκτης (trṓktēs, “nibbler”), from τρώγω (trṓgō, “to gnaw”), from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“to rub, to turn”). The Internet verb sense originated on BBSes of the 1980s, probably from Monty Python's The Fish-Slapping Dance (1972), though that sketch involved a halibut.

senses.d: Any of several species of fish in Salmonidae, closely related to salmon, and distinguished by spawning more than once.
ex: Many anglers consider trout to be the archetypical quarry.
“This morning,” he said, “We will fish, Turner. We will cast for trout so that we may catch grayling.”

senses.d: An objectionable elderly woman.
ex: Look, you silly old trout, you can't keep bringing home cats! You can't afford the ones you have!

senses.d: To fish for trout.
To (figuratively) slap someone with a slimy, stinky, wet trout; to admonish jocularly.

ety.text: Verb is from Middle English troublen, trouble, borrowed from Old French troubler, trobler, trubler, metathetic variants of tourbler, torbler, turbler, from Vulgar Latin *turbulō, from Latin turbula (“disorderly group, a little crowd or people”), diminutive of turba (“stir; crowd”). The noun is from Middle English trouble, troble, from Old French troble, from the verb.

senses.d: A distressing or dangerous situation.
ex: He was in trouble when the rain started.

senses.d: A difficulty, problem, condition, or action contributing to such a situation.
ex: The trouble was a leaking brake line.
The bridge column magnified the trouble with a slight tilt in the wrong direction.

senses.d: A person liable to place others or themselves in such a situation.
ex:
Get me on the court and I'm trouble
Last week, messed around and got a triple double

’Cause I knew you were trouble when you walked in
So shame on me no-ow

senses.d: The state of being troubled, disturbed, or distressed mentally; unease, disquiet.
Objectionable feature of something or someone; problem, drawback, weakness, failing, or shortcoming.
ex: Your trouble is that you quit too readily.
The trouble with that suggestion is that we lack the funds to put it in motion.

senses.d: Violent or turbulent occurrence or event; unrest, disturbance.
ex: the troubles in Northern Ireland

senses.d: Efforts taken or expended, typically beyond the normal required.
ex: It’s no trouble for me to edit it.
She never took the trouble to close them.

senses.d: Difficulty in doing something.
ex: She has trouble eating.

senses.d: Health problems, ailment, generally of some particular part of the body.
ex: He’s been in hospital with some heart trouble.

senses.d: A malfunction.
ex: My old car has engine trouble.

senses.d: To disturb, stir up, agitate (a medium, especially water).
ex: For an Angel went downe at a certaine season into the poole, and troubled the water:
God looking forth will trouble all his Hoſt

senses.d: To mentally distress; to cause (someone) to be anxious or perplexed.
ex: What she said about narcissism is troubling me.
Now is my soule troubled, and what shall I say? Father, saue me from this houre, but for this cause came I vnto this houre.

senses.d: In weaker sense: to bother or inconvenience.
ex: I will not trouble you to deliver the letter.

senses.d: To physically afflict.
ex: My bad knee is troubling me.

senses.d: To take pains (to do something); to bother.
ex: I won’t trouble to post the letter today; I can do it tomorrow.
« The hut’s not very tidy, if you don’t mind, » he said. « I cleared it what I could. » / « But I didn’t want you to trouble! » she said.

senses.d: To worry; to be anxious.
ex: Why trouble about the future? It is wholly uncertain.

A small wheel; specifically (fishing), the reel or winch of a fishing line.
A trolley.
